Gives: Remove 1 card of your choice from the deck (not a Mythic) and gain +1 slot
Lore: Astronauts throw away or cannibalise anything that doesn't earn its place in the cabin.

Gives: Replace 1 card with a random card of the same rarity
Risks / What Can Happen: The new card can be worse. The bad Commons like the Plastic Jug are in the pool
Lore: Swapping parts at the last minute before launch is a gamble, as the original sellers know.

Gives: 3 random cards, at least 1 of them Rare
Risks / What Can Happen: The other 2 cards can be of any rarity, Mythic included, and can be the bad ones
Lore: A box of unlabelled surplus gear bought at auction without opening it.

Gives: Remove 1 card and gain +2 slots
Costs: You lose the removed card's effect for the whole run
Lore: The ISS crews routinely strip one dead module to repair another.

Gives: +3 slots
Costs: +6 t mass, which makes take-off harder
Lore: Extra storage always weighs something, and the rocket has to lift it.

Gives: Duplicate 1 Common card already in your deck
Lore: The ISS has had a 3D printer since 2014 and prints its own tools and spare parts.

Gives: Trade 2 Common cards for 1 random Rare
Risks / What Can Happen: The Rare is random, so it may not fit your build
Lore: Logistics officers are always trying to turn a pile of junk into one good part.

Gives: 50% chance of 2 random Rare cards, 50% chance of losing 2 random cards
Risks / What Can Happen: The loss can hit your key cards
Lore: Some crews bet the whole cargo on a single resupply.

Gives: +2 slots
Lore: A perfect packing plan, with every module fitted so that none disturbs another.

Gives: Add 1 random Mythic to your deck
Lore: New hardware flies on trust in the engineers until the first real test.

Gives: +4 Morale per turn (cumulative: every copy adds its own bonus)
Risks / What Can Happen: 20% chance per turn of radio interference: the bonus is lost and the crew takes -3 Morale from the silence. Chance rises to 30% if placed next to the Energy card
Synergy / Impact: Stacks with all Communication cards; each copy rolls its own interference. Bad adjacency with Energy
Lore: Amateur radio has flown on the ISS for years (ARISS) and lets astronauts chat with schoolkids and hobbyists. Consumer-grade handhelds were never shielded for a crowded spacecraft: electromagnetic interference from power lines makes them crackle, drop out and drive the crew mad.

Gives: +12 Morale per turn (cumulative with other Communication cards). Isolation events cost 25% less Morale
Synergy / Impact: Halves the interference chance of Common Communication cards. Stacks with all Communication cards
Lore: Real crews get scheduled private video calls with their families and private medical and psychological conferences, relayed through data satellites (TDRS on the ISS). Seeing loved ones is one of the best countermeasures against isolation on long missions.

Card Name: Deep Space Optical Communications Terminal (Laser Uplink)
Gives: +35 Morale per turn (cumulative with other Communication cards). Crew Morale can never fall below 25. Immune to all communication blackouts and failures
Synergy / Impact: +10 Morale per turn extra if a Navigation card is in play (precise laser pointing). Cancels every Communication risk
Lore: NASA's DSOC experiment on the Psyche mission (2023) proved that a laser can carry data across tens of millions of kilometres at far higher rates than radio. Extrapolated here to endless HD calls, music and live Earth broadcasts, which makes the crew feel they never left home.

Gives: Reduces the chance of Hazard events appearing by 10%
Risks / What Can Happen: 35% chance per turn of losing the satellite fix: the reduction is lost and the chance of Hazard events appearing is +10% instead (the app steers you into the debris)
Synergy / Impact: Reductions from Navigation cards add up (suggested cap: -75%)
Lore: Consumer GPS receivers lock out above a speed and altitude limit (export-control limits) and were built to follow roads, not orbits. Past Earth orbit the app keeps announcing "recalculating" and confidently sends you the wrong way.

Gives: Reduces the chance of Hazard events appearing by 30%. Once per phase, reroll one drawn random event
Risks / What Can Happen: Sun glare blinds the star tracker 1 turn in 6: the Hazard reduction is halved that turn
Synergy / Impact: Reductions from Navigation cards add up (suggested cap: -75%). Draws on Energy
Lore: Spacecraft find their orientation by photographing star fields and matching them to a catalogue (star trackers), while gyroscopes and accelerometers (IMU) keep track of movement between photos. The combination is the backbone of real attitude and navigation systems.

Gives: Reduces the chance of Hazard events (debris, asteroids, micrometeoroids) appearing by 60%. Once every 6 turns, cancel one negative random event
Synergy / Impact: +10 Morale per turn if the Communication Mythic is also in play (ground control updates the course). Stacks with other Navigation cards, but total Hazard reduction is capped at -85%. Draws heavily on Energy
Lore: Deep Space 1 tested autonomous optical navigation (AutoNav) in 1998, and Perseverance landed using terrain-relative navigation. An onboard AI that watches the sky, tracks debris and re-plans the route without waiting for Earth makes the voyage far safer, but space still holds surprises.

Gives: +120 Thrust
Costs: Burns 60 Fuel at take-off. +4 t mass
Risks / What Can Happen: Cannot be throttled or shut down once lit
Lore: Solid boosters, like the Space Shuttle's reusable pair, deliver enormous thrust cheaply, but a solid motor burns until it is empty: you can neither throttle it nor switch it off.

Gives: +100 Thrust
Costs: Burns 50 Fuel at take-off. +3 t mass
Lore: The Soviet NK-33 was built for the N1 moon rocket in the 1960s. Decades later, leftover engines were refurbished and flew on commercial rockets, proof that old kerosene engines are cheap, heavy and reliable.

Gives: +260 Thrust
Costs: Burns 90 Fuel at take-off. +5 t mass
Synergy / Impact: Methane can be made on Mars (Sabatier reaction): pairs with the Oxygen Mythic
Lore: Staged-combustion engines burn their propellants completely and reach very high efficiency and chamber pressure. Methane and liquid oxygen is the fuel mix of choice for reusable rockets and Mars missions.

Gives: +150 Thrust
Costs: Burns 35 Fuel at take-off. +2 t mass
Synergy / Impact: Very fuel-efficient: best Thrust per Fuel in the deck outside the Mythic
Lore: Hydrogen and oxygen engines have the best specific impulse of any chemical rocket, which is why they power the upper stages of many launchers. The catch is that hydrogen is very bulky, so the tanks are huge.

Gives: +600 Thrust
Costs: Burns 150 Fuel at take-off. +12 t mass
Synergy / Impact: Highest Thrust per Fuel and per tonne in the game
Lore: Clustering dozens of engines under a single stage is the way to launch the heaviest payloads ever built. The N1 failed because of the complexity of its cluster; modern engine controllers can shut down a failed engine and keep climbing.

Gives: +60 Fuel
Lore: The cheapest way to carry propellant is in simple steel drums. They are easy to find and load, but drums and valves are never perfectly sealed.

Gives: +100 Fuel
Lore: Kerosene (RP-1) is dense, cheap and easy to store, so a simple welded tank does the job with no special handling.

Gives: +200 Fuel
Synergy / Impact: Best paired with Hydrogen or Methalox engines
Lore: Aluminium-lithium alloy is lighter and stronger than ordinary aluminium, and was used for the giant external tank of the Space Shuttle. Cryogenic propellants slowly boil away even in insulated tanks.

Gives: +150 Fuel
Synergy / Impact: Safer than the cryogenic tank: no boil-off
Lore: Carbon-fibre overwrapped tanks hold high pressure reliably and do not leak or boil off. Spacecraft use them for gas and propellant storage because they are tough and light.

Gives: +450 Fuel
Synergy / Impact: Largest Fuel reserve in the game
Lore: Chilling propellants well below their boiling point makes them denser, so more fits in the same volume. Orbital propellant depots and densified propellant are key technologies for deep space and Mars missions.
